title: The Goddess at the Table
hookLine: night eight: Mahagauri, the bright one, and young girls are welcomed in, their feet washed, and served as the goddess
carry: the goddess dwells in every being

last: LEARNING IS SOMETHING YOU BOW TO.

lines: THE GIRLS FROM DOWN THE STREET.
cards: The doorbell rings, and it's the girls from down the street, a little shy, in their best clothes. Inside, the grown-ups have been cooking since early: puris, a sweet semolina halwa, spiced chickpeas.

The girls sit in a row. An aunt kneels and washes their feet, dabs a red mark on each forehead, ties a red thread on each wrist. They're served first, before anyone else eats, and they leave with a small gift.
In parts of North India this is kanya puja, or kanjak, kept on the eighth or ninth day. For a morning, the goddess is the girl next door.

teach.b: The eighth name in the Kavacha's list is Mahagauri. It means the great Gauri, and Gauri is a name of Parvati, the bright one. On this night she's shown dressed in white, calm, shining.
There's a story people tell about it. Parvati did hard austerities for a long time to win Shiva, out in the sun and the rain, until her body was darkened with dust and weather.
When Shiva finally accepted her, he washed her with the water of the Ganga, and she came out shining.
So the bright form is what's left after long effort, washed clean. Now hold that next to the morning with the girls. Usually children touch their elders' feet.

teach.h: THE ELDERS WASH THE GIRLS' FEET.
teach.b: In kanya puja the elders wash the children's feet, and the aunts and grandmothers serve the girls first. Behind it is one of the best-known hymns of the Devi Mahatmya, one many families chant in these nights.
The gods praise the goddess who dwells in all beings: as consciousness, as sleep, as hunger, as mercy, as mother. And each time they bow, again and again. That's the teaching kanya puja acts out.

The goddess isn't only in the temple or on the altar. She dwells in every being, and for one morning a house practices seeing her in the smallest people at its table. Mahagauri is brightness after long effort.
Kanya puja is learning to see that brightness in a child.

how: In parts of North India, families keep kanya puja (kanjak) on the eighth or ninth day of Navaratri, washing the feet of young girls, feeding them puri, halwa and chickpeas, and giving them small gifts; where the nine forms are kept, the eighth night honors Mahagauri.

games.q: it's the eighth morning. the girls from down the street are at your table, and the food is ready. who eats first?
games.why: the girls eat first, served by their elders. the goddess honored for eight nights is honored in them.

practice: Bring to mind a child or a young person you know, a niece, a neighbor's kid, a student, your own, and see their face.
Instead of the usual thoughts, homework, screen time, behavior, look at them the way the aunts look at the girls at kanya puja: as someone worth serving, with the goddess living in them.
If you pray, you can quietly say the hymn's refrain over them, namas tasyai, salutations to her, or hold them before God in your own words. If you don't, simply wish them well by name.
